case_analysis.focal_point: Whether wetlands on the Sacketts’ property qualify as “waters of the United States” under the Clean Water Act—triggering federal permitting—based on their connection (or lack of it) to traditionally navigable waters.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. §§ 1251 et seq., particularly § 1362(7) (defining “navigable waters” as “the waters of the United States”) and the Act’s § 404 dredge-and-fill permitting framework (33 U.S.C. § 1344).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the agencies and the Ninth Circuit adopted an unlawfully broad test for Clean Water Act jurisdiction over wetlands, extending federal power to land that is not part of (and not sufficiently connected to) traditional waters. Relying on the post-Rapanos split, they contend the Court should reject Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” approach and instead require a clearer, more limited jurisdictional rule (closer to the Rapanos plurality) that confines federal regulation to relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection to such waters, emphasizing fair notice, limits on federal power, and the practical burdens on landowners (including homebuilding, forestry, agriculture, and similar land uses).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Congress intended broad Clean Water Act coverage to protect downstream water quality and aquatic integrity, and that wetlands like those at issue fall within federal jurisdiction when they significantly affect traditional navigable waters (the “significant nexus” framework associated with Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence). They maintain that lower courts properly treated Rapanos as allowing jurisdiction where either the plurality test or the significant-nexus test is met, and that this approach best implements the Act’s text, purpose, and scientific realities of hydrological and ecological connectivity—consistent with robust protection supported by conservation and outdoor recreation interests.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point—that a continuous-surface-connection rule can be evaded by berms or culverts and may miss wetlands that materially affect downstream waters—but under a penalty-backed statute we cannot let purpose supply an open-ended jurisdictional trigger untethered to the term “waters.” Justice Jackson’s suggestion that agencies could cure notice concerns with better procedures under a significant-nexus regime does not answer the core rule-of-law defect: the test itself invites case-by-case ecological line-drawing with no stable stopping point, and the fair-notice problem persists even with improved process. On precedent, I agree with Justice Barrett (and Justice Kavanaugh) that Marks cannot legitimately elevate Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence into controlling law where neither rationale is a true subset, so we must adopt the best, administrable reading of the statute rather than select among noncontrolling tests. A relatively permanent water plus continuous surface connection standard is narrower and more workable, and Congress remains free to expand coverage explicitly if it chooses.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that “waters of the United States” is supposedly ambiguous and should be implemented through an effects-based “significant nexus” inquiry, but that argument elevates statutory purpose and agency discretion over the ordinary meaning of “waters” and the federalism-sensitive limitation Congress retained by using “navigable waters.” Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Marks is unpersuasive here because, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, the Rapanos plurality’s continuous-surface-connection test and Justice Kennedy’s significant-nexus test are not logical subsets; Marks cannot be used to manufacture an “either/or” regime that effectively authorizes jurisdiction untethered to the statutory text. Even if wetlands can influence downstream quality, the question is what Congress enacted: a law regulating “waters,” not any land with ecological effects, and the significant-nexus test invites precisely the boundless, case-by-case expansion Rapanos warned against. On this record, the Sacketts’ wetlands lack the kind of continuous surface connection that would make them part of covered “waters,” so § 404 permitting authority does not attach.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that “waters of the United States” is open-textured and should be read in light of the Act’s purposes, with Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” test supplying a limiting principle. But purpose cannot expand the statutory term “waters” to encompass lands lacking a clear physical connection; as Justice Roberts notes, that approach has produced persistent confusion and undermines fair notice in a regime backed by severe penalties, effectively turning the CWA into an amorphous land-use code. Nor does Marks compel adopting Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling here, because—consistent with the Chief’s observation—the plurality’s continuous-surface-connection rule and the significant-nexus test are not nested “narrowest grounds,” so elevating Kennedy’s standard is a choice about policy, not about binding precedent. On a textualist, administrable reading, wetlands are covered only when they are effectively part of covered waters via a direct physical connection, which is absent here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s fair-notice and administrability concerns carry real weight in a penalty-backed statute, and Justice Barrett is right that Marks does not mechanically yield a controlling opinion from Rapanos when the rationales are not nested. But that only means we must choose the best reading of “waters of the United States,” and a rigid “continuous surface connection” rule is an underinclusive proxy that predictably invites evasion through trivial separations while leaving the same downstream pollution and flooding harms Congress targeted in § 1251(a). Justice Kennedy’s significant-nexus approach—properly cabined to demonstrable, significant effects on traditionally navigable waters and enforced with clear agency criteria and reviewable findings—better honors the statute’s structure (including Congress’s treatment of adjacent wetlands) without collapsing into boundless discretion. Under my pragmatic approach, the rule-of-law response to notice problems is to demand objective, consistently applied nexus standards, not to adopt a formalistic line that externalizes harms onto downstream communities, often the most vulnerable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice critique is the petitioners’ strongest point, and in a civil/criminal statute we should insist that any jurisdictional test be stated in objective, reviewable terms rather than open-ended ecological generalities. But the “continuous surface connection” rule pressed by Justices Alito, Barrett, and Gorsuch reads “adjacent wetlands” and the Act’s § 404 design too narrowly by making coverage turn on easily engineered surface features even when wetlands functionally affect downstream traditionally navigable waters—an outcome hard to square with ordinary usage of “adjacent” and the statute’s integrated permitting scheme. On Marks, I agree with Roberts and Barrett that Rapanos is not a clean subset case, so Kennedy is not mechanically controlling; still, the better textual-and-structural reading is a cabined significant-nexus standard that ties “waters” to demonstrable, significant effects on traditional navigable waters while requiring agencies to articulate clear criteria to satisfy notice concerns. That approach preserves statutory coherence and administrability without converting the CWA into either a boundless land-use code or an underinclusive proxy that invites evasion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that the Act’s broad purpose “to restore and maintain” water integrity and Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” test would capture wetlands that materially affect downstream waters. But purpose cannot dissolve the statutory limit Congress chose—“waters of the United States” naturally denotes actual waters, not any land feature with an ecologically arguable relationship, and a case-by-case nexus test risks transferring lawmaking to agencies and depriving landowners of fair notice in a regime with serious penalties. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Marks provides no stable answer in Rapanos because neither the plurality nor Kennedy is a logical subset of the other, so we must adopt the best reading of the statute rather than pretend a controlling opinion exists. On that reading, wetlands are covered only when they are part of covered waters through a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters, which the Sacketts lack.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the strongest case that a continuous-surface-connection rule can be evaded by engineered berms or minor separations while leaving downstream harms unchanged, but under my rule-of-law and federalism methodology that policy concern cannot justify an open-ended jurisdictional trigger backed by severe civil and criminal penalties. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Marks does not legitimately elevate Justice Kennedy’s significant-nexus concurrence in Rapanos to controlling law because neither rationale is a logical subset of the other, and the ensuing instability in lower courts underscores the fair-notice problem. Even if agencies could adopt better procedures under a nexus regime (Justice Jackson’s point), the statute’s text—“waters”—and history support a more determinate line tied to physical integration with relatively permanent waters, leaving Congress to speak more clearly if it wishes to extend § 404 further. I therefore remain with the petitioner on adopting a continuous-surface-connection requirement as the best administrable, legitimacy-preserving interpretation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson press the strongest point that a continuous-surface-connection rule can be underinclusive and invite evasion by minor engineered barriers, but that critique ultimately targets consequences and administrability rather than the original public meaning of “waters,” which denotes discrete bodies of water rather than any land with downstream effects. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s Marks analysis is persuasive: because the Rapanos plurality and Justice Kennedy’s concurrence are not logical subsets, treating “significant nexus” as controlling is not faithful application of precedent but a choice of an open-ended standard that aggravates fair-notice concerns in a penalty-backed scheme. The Act’s purpose in § 1251(a) may guide interpretation at the margins, yet it cannot supply atextual authority to regulate wetlands lacking a clear physical integration with covered waters. On this record, absent a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters, the wetlands are not part of “waters of the United States.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice and administrability concerns carry real weight in a penalty-backed scheme, but his continuous-surface-connection rule treats a physical-contiguity proxy as if it were the statute’s limit, even where wetlands functionally protect downstream navigable waters and can be separated by trivial, easily engineered barriers. Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett are right that Marks does not mechanically crown Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence as controlling; that point matters for stare decisis hygiene, but it does not resolve the best reading of “waters of the United States,” especially given Congress’s specific attention to “adjacent wetlands” in the § 404 context. Under a pragmatic, fairness-centered approach, the answer to notice problems is not an underinclusive bright line that invites evasion and externalizes flooding and pollution harms, but a significant-nexus inquiry cabined by objective, consistently applied agency criteria, evidentiary burdens, and robust procedures to ensure reviewable, non-arbitrary jurisdictional determinations. Justice Gorsuch’s ordinary-meaning framing also underreads how the Act’s design contemplates regulating fill in wetlands when they operate as part of the aquatic system affecting navigable waters, so the land/water dichotomy cannot do all the work.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s text—defining “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7)—must be applied with administrable limits that provide fair notice and avoid an assertion of boundless federal authority over land and water features traditionally regulated by the States. Rapanos v. United States fractured the Court, and Marks v. United States offers no stable “narrowest grounds” when the plurality’s “continuous surface connection/relatively permanent waters” approach and Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” test are not true subsets of one another, a circumstance that has produced persistent confusion and threatens institutional legitimacy. To restore clarity on narrow grounds, I would adopt a more definite jurisdictional rule requiring wetlands to have a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters that are themselves connected to traditionally navigable waters, rather than an open-ended “significant nexus” inquiry. On that understanding, wetlands like the Sacketts’—lacking such a surface connection—do not fall within § 404 permitting jurisdiction under 33 U.S.C. § 1344.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s text extends federal authority only to “navigable waters,” defined as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and that phrase cannot be read—consistent with ordinary meaning and federalism limits—to cover wetlands lacking a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters. Rapanos v. United States rejects purpose-driven, case-by-case expansions of jurisdiction untethered to statutory text, and Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” approach invites precisely that sort of boundless administrative discretion. Marks v. United States does not justify an “either/or” regime that effectively allows the Rapanos dissent to control by combining votes; the controlling rule must reflect a grounded limitation on what counts as “waters,” not an open-ended ecological-effects test. Because the Sacketts’ wetlands are not part of, and lack a continuous surface connection to, traditionally navigable waters or their relatively permanent tributaries, § 404 permitting cannot be triggered here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and that text cannot fairly be stretched to cover wetlands lacking a clear, physical connection to traditionally navigable waters; otherwise the Act becomes an open-ended land-use code enforced through severe penalties. Rapanos v. United States supports a narrower, administrable jurisdictional rule: wetlands are covered only when they are adjacent in the sense of having a continuous surface (or similarly direct physical) connection to relatively permanent waters, avoiding the indeterminate, litigation-driven “significant nexus” inquiry. Marks v. United States does not compel treating Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling where, as in Rapanos, no single rationale is a true “narrowest grounds” common denominator, and the significant-nexus approach has generated substantial regulatory uncertainty and unfair notice problems for ordinary property owners. Practical consequences also favor Petitioners: an unclear test that expands federal permitting under § 404, 33 U.S.C. § 1344, invites arbitrary enforcement and undermines predictable rules needed for lawful land development.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and Congress designed § 404 to protect downstream water quality and aquatic integrity from pollution and fill even when harms originate in adjacent or nearby wetlands. In a fractured Court, Marks v. United States instructs that the controlling rule is the position taken on the narrowest grounds, and Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence—requiring a “significant nexus” between wetlands and traditionally navigable waters—best implements the Act’s protective purpose while providing a workable limitation grounded in real hydrological and ecological effects. That standard recognizes that wetlands can materially affect downstream waters by filtering pollutants and mitigating flooding, aligning with the Act’s objective “to restore and maintain” the integrity of the Nation’s waters, 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). Given those practical impacts—especially on communities vulnerable to degraded water quality—the agencies may assert jurisdiction when the requisite significant nexus is shown.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and its core objective is to protect downstream water quality through a workable, coherent permitting scheme under § 404, 33 U.S.C. § 1344. In a fractured decision like Rapanos, Marks v. United States instructs that the controlling rule is the position on the narrowest grounds that would command a majority in most cases; lower courts reasonably treated Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” standard as that controlling approach because it captures wetlands that materially affect traditionally navigable waters while still requiring a limiting connection. That standard better fits the Act’s text and purpose than a rigid “continuous surface connection” rule, which risks excluding wetlands Congress meant to protect and undermining administrable, science-informed judgments by the responsible agencies. Given statutory ambiguity in “waters of the United States,” deference to the agencies’ reasonable nexus-based implementation supports sustaining jurisdiction here where the wetlands’ effects on downstream waters are substantial.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), a phrase that in ordinary meaning refers to actual waters—not any land that might bear some ecological relationship to them. Under Rapanos v. United States, the better reading—consistent with textual limits and separation-of-powers concerns—is that the Act reaches only relatively permanent bodies of water and, as to wetlands, those with a continuous surface connection to such waters, not a freestanding “significant nexus” standard that invites case-by-case administrative discretion. Expansive jurisdictional tests that turn on indeterminate ecological effects risk leaving regulated parties without fair notice and effectively transferring lawmaking to agencies, contrary to the statute Congress enacted. Because the Sacketts’ wetlands lack the requisite continuous surface connection to traditional waters, § 404 permitting authority under 33 U.S.C. § 1344 does not attach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1362(7) defines “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” and our precedents counsel a restrained, administrable construction that hews to the statute’s traditional focus on waters, not broadly on land use. Rapanos produced no clear majority, but the “significant nexus” approach has proven difficult for landowners and agencies to apply with fair notice and consistent results, undermining workability and the Court’s institutional interest in clear rules. Consistent with the Rapanos plurality’s emphasis on relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection to such waters, the Sacketts’ wetlands—lacking a continuous surface connection to traditional navigable waters—fall outside § 404 permitting jurisdiction. That reading respects history and tradition in federal regulation of navigable waters while leaving primary land-and-water-use authority with the States absent a clear congressional statement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and that text is best read—consistent with ordinary meaning and the Act’s structure—to cover traditional waters and wetlands only when they are effectively part of such waters, not merely ecologically related at some remove. Rapanos v. United States, 547 U.S. 715 (2006), did not yield a clear Marks v. United States, 430 U.S. 188 (1977), “controlling” standard that compels nationwide adoption of Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” test, and that test’s acknowledged indeterminacy raises serious fair-notice and administrability concerns in a permitting regime carrying significant civil and criminal consequences. A more textually anchored rule—requiring relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection to them (Rapanos plurality)—better cabins federal jurisdiction to what the statutory phrase “waters” can naturally bear while respecting precedent by applying a consistent, workable line. Because the Sacketts’ wetlands lack the requisite continuous surface connection to traditionally navigable waters, they do not qualify as “waters of the United States” triggering § 404 permitting under 33 U.S.C. § 1344.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s definition of “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), is textually open-ended and must be read in light of the Act’s objective to restore and maintain the integrity of the Nation’s waters, making it reasonable to cover wetlands whose functions materially affect downstream navigable waters through hydrological and ecological connections within the § 404 permitting scheme, 33 U.S.C. § 1344. In a fractured decision like Rapanos, Marks v. United States requires identifying the narrowest grounds that command a majority where possible; Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” framework supplies an administrable limiting principle that still serves Congress’s protective purpose better than a rigid “continuous surface connection” rule. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against abruptly narrowing jurisdiction in a way that would undermine water-quality protections and create incentives to evade regulation by severing surface connections while leaving real downstream harms intact. Given the CWA’s design and Rapanos’s recognition that wetlands may be jurisdictional when their effects on navigable waters are significant, the agencies’ approach is more consistent with the statute’s structure and Congress’s aims.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Clean Water Act’s term “waters of the United States” extends federal permitting jurisdiction to wetlands on private property that are not themselves traditional navigable waters but are allegedly connected to such waters.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Clean Water Act (33 U.S.C. §§ 1251 et seq.), especially § 301 (33 U.S.C. § 1311) and § 404 (33 U.S.C. § 1344), and the statutory phrase “navigable waters” defined as “waters of the United States” (33 U.S.C. § 1362(7)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Sacketts argue that the EPA/Corps have interpreted “waters of the United States” far too broadly—capturing wetlands and other features lacking a clear, surface-water connection to navigable waters—creating an unpredictable and constitutionally suspect regime that burdens ordinary land use; they press the Court to adopt a narrower, more administrable jurisdictional test (associated with the Rapanos plurality) requiring a relatively permanent water body and wetlands with a continuous surface connection to that water, rather than an open-ended ecological-effects inquiry.
case_analysis.respondent_position: EPA (and supporting amici) argue that Congress intended broad federal protection for aquatic systems and that wetlands adjacent or functionally connected to covered waters can be regulated to protect downstream water quality; they defend a jurisdictional approach consistent with Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” concept from Rapanos (and related agency guidance), under which wetlands fall within the Act when they significantly affect the chemical, physical, or biological integrity of traditional navigable waters.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson most forcefully argue that § 1251(a)’s “integrity” objective and watershed science demand an effects-based “significant nexus” test, and that a surface-connection rule can be evaded by berms or miss subsurface hydrology. But under my minimalist, institution-protective approach, purpose cannot supply the limiting principle where the operative text (“navigable waters” / “waters of the United States”) and § 404’s severe permitting and enforcement consequences require a clear, administrable boundary with fair notice; the very fact pattern-by-pattern ecology can justify jurisdiction is why we need a rule Congress clearly drew rather than one agencies and courts continuously elaborate. Justice Kagan’s point about the persistent Marks/Rapanos disarray confirms that treating Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling has not produced stability; moreover, as Justice Gorsuch underscores, Kennedy’s test is not a logical subset of the plurality’s, so Marks does not compel it. A narrow, text-tethered holding—covering wetlands only when they are adjacent to and have a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters, making them practically indistinguishable—respects federalism and leaves other wetlands to state regulation without foreclosing Congress from expanding coverage explicitly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that § 1251(a)’s broad purpose and downstream harms counsel an effects-based “significant nexus” test, but purpose cannot expand the enacted jurisdictional hook—“navigable waters,” defined as “waters of the United States”—beyond its ordinary meaning and the limiting work performed by “navigable.” An ecological-effects inquiry like “significant nexus” is not a textual boundary at all; it invites precisely the kind of unbounded federal police power over land use that the statute’s terms do not clearly authorize and that federalism canons counsel us to avoid absent a clear statement. Justice Gorsuch’s point about Marks confirms my view that we should not treat Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling when it is not a logical subset of the plurality and has produced doctrinal instability; we must instead interpret the statute directly and adopt a rule tethered to “waters,” i.e., relatively permanent waters and wetlands indistinguishable from them via a continuous surface connection. The civil/criminal consequences and pervasive state authority over local wetlands further reinforce the need for a clear, text-grounded limit rather than case-by-case agency discretion.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that § 1251(a)’s “integrity” objective and downstream harms counsel an effects-based “significant nexus” test, but purpose cannot expand “waters of the United States” beyond what the statutory text can bear—especially where § 404 permitting carries serious civil and criminal consequences requiring clear notice. As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan note, Marks has been unworkable in Rapanos: Kennedy’s “significant nexus” is not a logical subset of the plurality’s continuous-surface-connection rule, so it cannot be treated as controlling merely because lower courts found it attractive. The administrability and federalism concerns emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts reinforce that an open-ended ecological-effects inquiry would effectively federalize vast swaths of land-use regulation without a clear congressional statement. I therefore remain convinced that the statute is best read to cover only relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection making them practically indistinguishable from those waters.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan forcefully press administrability and fair-notice, but I do not think a continuous-surface-connection requirement is the only (or best) way to supply a limiting principle consistent with Congress’s design: the Act’s integrity-based objective and § 404’s function presume regulation of wetlands that materially affect downstream waters even when hydrology is seasonal, subsurface, or easily masked by a man-made berm. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers/lenity concern is better answered by insisting on a demanding evidentiary showing of a significant nexus and clearer agency standards, rather than adopting a rigid bright line that is both underinclusive (excluding wetlands that predictably drive flooding and pollution) and readily evaded. On precedent, while I accept the point Roberts and Kagan make that Marks does not mechanically produce a single controlling Rapanos rule, the widespread reliance on Justice Kennedy’s significant-nexus approach underscores its practicality as a cabined, effects-based standard tied to traditional navigable waters, not an unbounded federal police power. Under my pragmatic approach—focused on real-world consequences and access to justice—the petitioners’ rule would withdraw federal protection from communities downstream who bear the cumulative costs of incremental wetland loss, without a clearer textual command to do so.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right that § 1251(a)’s “integrity” objective and wetlands’ real downstream effects make an effects-sensitive standard attractive, and they correctly warn that a surface-only line can be underinclusive or evadable by berms. But under a pragmatic textualist reading, that purpose cannot do the jurisdiction-defining work that Congress tied to “waters of the United States,” § 1362(7), in a scheme carrying serious permitting burdens and criminal exposure; as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, we need a stable, administrable boundary that gives fair notice and preserves the federal–state allocation. Justice Jackson’s proposal to cabin “significant nexus” through evidentiary demands does not cure the core defect: it still makes coverage turn on open-ended ecological judgments case by case, which (as our Rapanos experience shows) has generated persistent disuniformity and invites jurisdiction to expand without a clear textual stopping point. I therefore continue to think the best text-tethered, workable middle ground is covering wetlands that are functionally part of covered waters—i.e., adjacent with a continuous surface connection making them practically indistinguishable—while leaving substantial regulation of other wetlands to the States.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the Act’s broad purpose to protect the “integrity” of the Nation’s waters, but purpose cannot supply jurisdictional boundaries the text withholds—especially where “navigable waters” and the § 404 scheme demand a discernible, administrable limit for landowners and States. The “significant nexus” test she and Justice Jackson defend effectively delegates to agencies a case-by-case power to define the statute’s reach, a separation-of-powers problem magnified by the CWA’s severe civil and potential criminal consequences and the resulting fair-notice concerns. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Marks does not force us to treat Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence as controlling when it is not a logical subset of the plurality’s rationale, and lower-court confusion confirms the absence of any true “narrowest grounds.” The better course is to decide the statute’s meaning directly and adopt the text-tethered line requiring relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection, which supplies clear limits consistent with ordinary meaning and federalism.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make their strongest case by tying “waters of the United States” to the Act’s integrity purpose and arguing that subsurface/seasonal connections mean an effects-based “significant nexus” test is the only practical way to protect downstream waters; but as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, purpose cannot supply the jurisdictional line where the statute’s text and the § 404 permitting/criminal-enforcement structure demand clear notice and an administrable boundary. I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch that Marks does not compel adopting Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence because it is not a logical subset of the plurality rule, and the resulting lower-court disuniformity is itself evidence that “significant nexus” lacks the stable limiting principle this federalism-sensitive scheme requires. The underinclusiveness/evading-berms concern is a policy argument better directed to Congress and the States; our job is to interpret “waters” in a way that cabins federal power to relatively permanent waters and wetlands that are functionally part of them through a continuous surface connection. No colleague has identified statutory text or controlling precedent that squarely authorizes extending federal jurisdiction based solely on ecological effects absent that kind of water-like connection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that § 1251(a)’s “integrity” objective and the reality of subsurface and seasonal hydrology suggest Congress meant to reach wetlands with substantial downstream effects even absent a surface connection. But under a textualist methodology, that purposive backdrop cannot expand the operative jurisdictional term—“waters of the United States,” § 1362(7)—beyond its ordinary public meaning; an effects-based “significant nexus” inquiry risks converting “waters” into a policy-driven standard limited only by expert judgment rather than statutory text. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Marks does not compel adoption of Justice Kennedy’s Rapanos concurrence because it is not a logical subset of the plurality’s rationale, and the resulting lower-court instability reinforces the notice and federalism problems of a case-by-case regime under §§ 301 and 404. The better text-anchored, administrable line remains wetlands that are functionally part of covered waters—i.e., adjoining wetlands with a continuous surface connection rendering them practically indistinguishable from relatively permanent waters—leaving other wetlands to state regulation absent clearer congressional direction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s administrability/fair-notice concerns are the strongest pushback, but I do not think a continuous-surface-connection prerequisite is meaningfully more text-grounded than an effects-based inquiry given Congress’s express focus on protecting the downstream “chemical, physical, and biological integrity” of covered waters. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers/lenity point also matters, yet it cuts toward requiring a rigorous evidentiary showing and clearer agency articulation of what constitutes a “significant nexus,” not toward categorically excluding wetlands that demonstrably and substantially affect navigable waters through known hydrologic pathways. On precedent, I agree with Justice Kagan that Marks has not yielded a stable controlling rule from Rapanos, but that only means we must choose the best reading of the statute now—and I remain persuaded that a cabined significant-nexus standard better matches the Act’s structure and practical consequences than a bright line that is easily evaded and underprotective of downstream communities. In my view, procedural fairness is served by demanding proof of substantial downstream impact and reasoned agency explanations, rather than by adopting an atextual surface-connection rule that can deny coverage to functionally critical wetlands.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and the Act’s structure—especially § 404’s permitting regime—counsels an interpretation that gives regulated parties clear notice and preserves a meaningful limiting principle tied to the statute’s navigation-linked term. Given the fractured decision in Rapanos v. United States (2006) and the difficulty of applying Marks v. United States (1977) to extract a single controlling rationale, I would adopt a narrow, administrable jurisdictional rule requiring wetlands to be adjacent to covered waters with a continuous surface connection, rather than an open-ended “significant nexus” inquiry that risks case-by-case unpredictability and federalism concerns. That approach better protects institutional legitimacy by providing stable guidance, respects the States’ traditional authority over land and water use, and avoids expanding federal jurisdiction beyond what Congress clearly authorized. On this record, wetlands on private property lacking a continuous surface-water connection to traditional navigable waters fall outside federal permitting jurisdiction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Clean Water Act regulates “navigable waters,” defined as “the waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7); read in light of the statutory term “navigable” and the Act’s text, that phrase cannot be stretched to reach any wetland that merely bears an ecological relationship to downstream waters. Section 404’s permitting scheme, 33 U.S.C. § 1344, must be limited to wetlands that are part of, or indistinguishable from, covered waters—i.e., those with a continuous surface connection to a relatively permanent body of water—otherwise the agencies’ “significant nexus” approach becomes an atextual, boundless assertion of federal police power over private land use. Rapanos v. United States (2006) supports this narrower, administrable reading by rejecting open-ended jurisdiction untethered to the ordinary meaning of “waters,” and any broader construction would also raise serious federalism concerns by displacing traditional state authority over land and water resources without clear congressional statement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Clean Water Act regulates “navigable waters,” defined as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1344, 1362(7), and that text is best read to reach only relatively permanent bodies of water and wetlands that have a continuous surface connection to such waters, not remote wetlands connected only by speculative ecological effects. Rapanos v. United States (2006) exposes the administrability and notice problems of an open-ended “significant nexus” test, which risks converting federal permitting into a boundless, case-by-case inquiry untethered from statutory text and imposing severe practical burdens on ordinary landowners. Marks v. United States (1977) does not justify the agencies’ “either/or” amalgam of a concurrence with a dissent to expand jurisdiction beyond what any single rationale commanding the judgment supports, and the Court should adopt a clearer, narrower rule that better cabins federal power. Given the practical consequences of criminal and civil enforcement under the CWA, a bright-line, text-grounded jurisdictional test is necessary to provide fair notice and avoid overbroad federal intrusion into traditional state land-use authority.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s objective is to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters,” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a), and Congress empowered federal permitting to prevent discharges that degrade downstream waters, including through § 404 wetlands regulation, 33 U.S.C. § 1344. In a fractured Rapanos, lower courts applying Marks v. United States have treated Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as the controlling standard, because his “significant nexus” test captures wetlands that meaningfully affect traditional navigable waters’ integrity without adopting the plurality’s rigid surface-connection requirement. That approach better implements the Act’s remedial structure by protecting vulnerable downstream communities from pollution and flooding harms that often flow from incremental wetland losses. Accordingly, where the government shows a significant nexus between the wetlands and covered waters, federal jurisdiction is consistent with the statute and precedent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Clean Water Act defines “navigable waters” as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and that text—read in light of the Act’s structure and federalism-sensitive permitting scheme in §§ 1311 and 1344—signals limits that must be administrable for regulated parties and state partners. Rapanos produced no majority, and Marks has proved unworkable as applied there: lower courts have splintered over whether Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” is controlling, which itself underscores that the test does not supply a clear, judicially manageable boundary for jurisdiction. A narrower, text-tethered approach focused on wetlands that are meaningfully part of covered “waters” (i.e., adjacent to relatively permanent waters with a continuous surface connection) better promotes statutory coherence and workability while still leaving room for robust state regulation of isolated wetlands. Accordingly, I would reject an open-ended ecological-effects inquiry as the governing standard and vote to limit federal jurisdiction to wetlands that are functionally indistinguishable from covered waters.

Rapanos v. United States rejected open-ended approaches untethered to discernible statutory limits, and the “significant nexus” test lacks administrable, text-based boundaries and invites case-by-case agency policymaking with substantial separation-of-powers costs. Marks v. United States does not compel treating Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling where no opinion supplies a true “narrowest grounds” that is a logical subset of the other; instead, the Court should adopt a clear rule consistent with the statutory text—requiring a relatively permanent water body and wetlands with a continuous surface connection to it. Any lingering ambiguity in the scope of a statute carrying severe civil and potential criminal consequences should be resolved narrowly, consistent with fair notice principles and the rule of lenity.

Rapanos v. United States (2006) failed to yield a workable, precedentially stable rule under Marks v. United States (1977), and the agencies’ post-Rapanos “either/or” approach (treating both the plurality and Justice Kennedy’s concurrence as controlling) exacerbates unpredictability and undermines administrability for ordinary property owners. A jurisdictional test tied to relatively permanent waters and wetlands with a continuous surface connection better fits the statutory focus on “waters,” accords with precedent’s emphasis on clear limits, and promotes practical workability by reducing case-by-case ecological effects inquiries. Accordingly, the CWA does not extend federal permitting jurisdiction to the Sacketts’ wetlands absent that continuous surface connection to traditional navigable waters or their covered tributaries.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Clean Water Act regulates “navigable waters,” defined as “waters of the United States,” 33 U.S.C. § 1362(7), and the ordinary meaning of “waters” does not naturally encompass wetlands lacking a continuous surface connection to a relatively permanent body of water. Reading § 301 and § 404 (33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1344) to reach any wetland with ecological effects on downstream waters risks substituting statutory purpose for text and invites an indeterminate, case-by-case regime that strains federal power and fair notice. Rapanos’s plurality provides the more administrable, text-anchored line—requiring a relatively permanent water and wetlands indistinguishable from it via a continuous surface connection—whereas Justice Kennedy’s “significant nexus” test is untethered to the statutory term “waters” and has proved difficult to apply. Marks v. United States does not compel adopting the “significant nexus” approach here because Rapanos lacks a true “narrowest grounds” common denominator that lower courts can reliably extract into a controlling rule, so the Court should decide the meaning of the statute directly.

In Rapanos v. United States (2006), Justice Kennedy’s concurrence supplies an administrable, effects-based limitation—requiring a “significant nexus” to traditional navigable waters—which lower courts have treated as controlling under Marks v. United States (1977) in many applications and which aligns with the agencies’ long-standing implementation. That approach better advances procedural fairness and practical consequences by focusing jurisdiction on meaningful downstream impacts rather than formalistic hydrologic labels that can under-protect water quality. Given the longstanding reliance on the significant-nexus framework and the statute’s remedial purpose, I would uphold the agencies’ authority to require permitting when that nexus is shown.
